correctness.rationale: The renewal identity is exact because position and OU velocity are both deterministically renewed. Girsanov and the passive killed spectral gap give local differentiability in active amplitude; differentiating the backward generator yields two linear Dirichlet–Neumann resolvent equations. Green inversion, passive polynomial factorization, the implicit-function theorem and exact sequential relaxation limits prove the single claim. 905 deterministic standard-library checks verify independent finite-difference solutions, polynomial limits, differential residuals, and opposite-sign coefficients; these are not treated as proof of infinite limits.

evidence: Pal–Reuveni (arXiv:1607.06048) derives the general renewal approach and coefficient-of-variation criterion used as Step 1; it does not calculate two fixed-launch OU first-passage moment perturbations.

Baouche–Kurzthaler (DOI:10.1039/D5SM00340G) analyzes initial orientation effects for a two-dimensional active Brownian searcher and unbounded wall geometry; the model differs from a one-dimensional OU velocity with a finite reflecting wall.
Shankari–Sahoo (arXiv:2509.18515) analyzes free-space active OU stochastic resetting through MSD and stationary distributions, not a bounded absorbing first-passage threshold.

Georgiou–Bressloff–Bertrand (arXiv:2609.21124v1) derives an analytic stationary-Gaussian velocity perturbation and numerically explores fixed-velocity resetting, leaving the exact deterministic-velocity coefficient untreated.

value.rationale: Source-identified fixed-velocity sensitivity had been evaluated through simulations. Exact first-order calibration and the limiting sign reversal identify a qualitative, physically motivated persistence boundary: outward initial velocity can expand, rather than always contract, the initially beneficial-reset region. This is an experimentally or numerically testable directional prediction and a mathematically natural boundary for protocol design, while staying local in reset rate and activity.
